newsitem.title: UK: Coffee - Prices firm on Colombia strike, tight supply.
newsitem.headline: Coffee - Prices firm on Colombia strike, tight supply.

text.p: Physical coffee prices remained firm this week, underpinned by continued tight nearby supplies and on news of a truck drivers' strike in key grower Colombia.
Traders said there was still good underlying demand for some robusta and washed arabica but very few deals were concluded due to a dearth of sellers.
"People are still picking up coffee but very little volume is being offered," said a London trader.
The Colombian truck drivers' nationwide strike entered its fourth day on Wednesday and there was still no clear sign that the stoppage would come to an end soon.

Union leaders said on Tuesday further talks were planned late on Wednesday but they stressed that little progress was expected unless the government acceded to demands for the establishment of minimum cargo rates.
Coffee rallied sharply in January on the crippling Colombian dockworkers strike. The truckers last went on strike in October which also halted coffee and other shipments.
Private Colombian exporters have warned that the workers' action could wreak havoc to coffee exports if it lasts more than 10 days.
The latest strike comes as Colombia's growers are just beginning to harvest the so-called "mitaca" crop, which accounts for about 40 percent of the yearly crop.
Colombian Excelso coffee prices were heard quoted at 30-35 U.S. cents a lb nominal over New York's July contract this week against 30 late last week.
"It's a sellers' market. Prices are all over the place," said another UK trader.
European roasters had replenished some of their stocks in the past few months and have not started any dramatic buying on the Colombian news.
But they would be forced to take cover and look for origins if the strike is prolonged and the supply pipeline is disrupted.
"People may start seeking alternatives to mainstream coffee from Colombia," said one trader. "But supplies from other areas are also tight."
